searchText: Dumb question: What's the significant advantage for removing? Final Proof size reduction?? Solos probably largely still with manual withdrawals at that point, or no withdrawals. The jump to 256 ETH is considerable. For someone like Lido it likely solves a lot. That allows a bond in 4 ETH steps, same as RocketPool currently. Likewise, institutionals who like liquidity have a great option there, for them 256, 512 etc is completely doable, even as 2048 may be a bridge too far for many of their clients. <@935504619554107392>, do you want to chime in? <@412614104222531604> grandine is ready for pq-devnet-0, we have it at https://github.com/grandinetech/grandine/tree/pq-devnet-0 I also made PR to add PQ support in [etherum-package](https://github.com/ethpandaops/eth-client-docker-image-builder/pull/440) and add docker files for [image builder](https://github.com/ethpandaops/eth-client-docker-image-builder/pull/440) I think the proof end up more or less the same size. I think the advantage is: you can do the recursive aggregation ahead of time (as aggregates arrive), adding total of one slot to the next. And then remove any included in the block. So when you get to your turn you have one additional aggregate to merge which has all attestations not added already. The removal seems to be generally cheaper than a recursive aggregation. or do you mean: why not just include all even if on chain already? I think as the number of claims in creases the cost of merging proofs goes up, but actually not sure actually it looks like the recursive merge cost is not greatly influenced the number of claims, e.g.: ``` recurse 16 -> 1: 16 proofs, 4929284 bytes, rate 1 -> proof 308376 bytes, 24000 claims, 1.817 s recurse 16 -> 1: 16 proofs, 2971956 bytes, rate 1 -> proof 284568 bytes, 2400 claims, 1.472 s ``` first case here has 10x more claims. so I guess the only advantage of removing is not to include repeats on chain. I’m gonna recommend migrating to a sidecar style solution for lean vm at least for now As right now pretty much every client uses a different commit hash for leanvm 🤣 so it’s kinda hard to get stuff working Are we already agree to use 0.15.0 for the devnet? Should we have devnet spec like before? yeah that’s what i thought Yeah i’ll put one together tomorrow Ya, if only a few bits are seen, I’d just keep the aggregate as is. If we can pick up a lot more bits, then pruning, replacing, or merging again might be worth it. I’m still thinking through how to balance attestation performance against prover load. I don’t have a clear heuristic yet <@412614104222531604> ethlambda is ready for `pq-devnet-0`. We published an image tagged `ghcr.io/lambdaclass/ethlambda:pq-devnet-0` (built from the [`pq-devnet-0` branch](https://github.com/lambdaclass/ethlambda/tree/pq-devnet-0) Dockerfile) and succesfully tested interop with Lighthouse, Teku, and Prysm in local devnets.

excerpts.author: yorickdowne
excerpts.content:
Solos probably largely still with manual withdrawals at that point, or no withdrawals. The jump to 256 ETH is considerable.

For someone like Lido it likely solves a lot. That allows a bond in 4 ETH steps, same as RocketPool currently.

Likewise, institutionals who like liquidity have a great option there, for them 256, 512 etc is completely doable, even as 2048 may be a bridge too far for many of their clients.

<@935504619554107392>, do you want to chime in?

excerpts.author: vladimir_ea
excerpts.content:
I think the proof end up more or less the same size. I think the advantage is: you can do the recursive aggregation ahead of time (as aggregates arrive), adding total of one slot to the next. And then remove any included in the block. So when you get to your turn you have one additional aggregate to merge which has all attestations not added already.

The removal seems to be generally cheaper than a recursive aggregation.

excerpts.author: vladimir_ea
excerpts.content: or do you mean: why not just include all even if on chain already? I think as the number of claims in creases the cost of merging proofs goes up, but actually not sure

excerpts.author: vladimir_ea
excerpts.content:
actually it looks like the recursive merge cost is not greatly influenced the number of claims, e.g.:
```
recurse 16 -> 1: 16 proofs, 4929284 bytes, rate 1 -> proof 308376 bytes, 24000 claims, 1.817 s
recurse 16 -> 1: 16 proofs, 2971956 bytes, rate 1 -> proof 284568 bytes, 2400 claims, 1.472 s
```
first case here has 10x more claims. 
so I guess the only advantage of removing is not to include repeats on chain.
